name: ETIGBUE ADAEZE CLARET
missingPieces: D1 catalogue omits stored XSS, path traversal, and the cookie missing Secure/SameSite finding; D2 omits the open-redirect hop and the forged super_admin scope-change insight; D3 mislabels open redirect as the decoy.
feedback: On D1 you built a clean evidence-first table and caught the core authentication stack well: SQL injection (A03, CWE-89) with both the concatenated $sql line and the admin' OR '1'='1 capture, the MD5 hashing (you wrote CWE-327 where CWE-916 is tighter, but the quoted line is right so I credited it), the hardcoded secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 (A02/A05, CWE-798), alg:none acceptance (you used CWE-345 where 347 is cleaner, accepted as a defensible variant), missing token expiry (CWE-613), open redirect (CWE-601) and XXE (CWE-611). Your decoy verdict is exactly right and is the strongest part of D1: you named hash_equals, proved it is a constant-time comparison so that branch is sound, and correctly pointed to alg:none and the hardcoded secret as the real bugs. What cost you on D1 is that the catalogue is not complete: stored XSS, path traversal to /etc/passwd, and the cookie missing Secure/SameSite are absent from the findings table even though XSS and path traversal show up later in D2 and D3, so each missing finding lost its share. On D2 your chain is reconciled to the capture timestamps in order (02:15:31 SQLi, 02:16:04 the 312 rows, 02:18:47 XSS, 02:24:02 path traversal, plus the parallel XXE and the exfil sample) and your verbatim PoC per hop is good, but you dropped the open redirect hop at 02:21:13 and you never made the senior point that the forged super_admin token reaches the shared /api/v1/internal service, which is the scope change. Your SQLi CVSS reads AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H, but the bypass does not affect availability, so it should be A:N giving roughly 9.1, not A:H; tighten that. Your impact cites 312 customers and the ₦950,000, ₦450,500.75 and ₦364,210.30 records, all of which trace to the exfil sample, so no fabrication, but you stopped short of summing the balances into the tens-of-millions headline and of stating your assumptions. D3 reads well for a CFO and ends on the customers-and-naira headline, the threat model and trust boundaries are sound, and your two detection stopgaps give exact scope, a regex field and a false-positive rate, which is what was asked. Two things hurt D3: you labelled the open redirect as the disproved decoy, which is wrong because the open redirect is a real finding and the actual safe construct is hash_equals (you had this right in D1, so this is just an inconsistency to fix), and your remediation list P1 to P5 is ordered by severity and chain position rather than by effort-to-risk, which caps that row. D4 is your strongest deliverable: you answer all four prompts in your own voice, cite ISC2 Canon 1 and Canon 2 by number in a load-bearing way, name NDPA 2023 Section 40 with the 72-hour NDPC duty tied to the 312 customers, and anchor to the incident, though adding Section 41 on notifying high-risk data subjects would have completed it. I looked hard for room to push this into the high 70s and the evidence did not support it, because three of the ten findings are simply not in the D1 catalogue and the remediation is severity-ordered. The single most important fix: complete the findings catalogue so stored XSS, path traversal and the cookie flags each get their own row with a quoted evidence line, because a partial catalogue is what kept this out of the 80s.
